# **Multimodal modelling of human emotion using sound, image and text** **fusion**
**Seyed Sadegh Hosseini** **[1]** **· Mohammad Reza Yamaghani** **[2]** **· Soodabeh Poorzaker Arabani** **[2]**
Received: 26 May 2023 / Revised: 2 July 2023 / Accepted: 14 July 2023 / Published online: 11 August 2023 © The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Springer-Verlag London Ltd., part of Springer Nature 2023
**Abstract**
Multimodal emotion recognition and analysis are considered as an evolving field of research. The improvement of the multimodal fusion mechanism plays an important role in the more detailed recognition of the recognised emotion. The performance of the emotion recognition system was optimised, and a model for multimodal emotion recognition from audio, text and video data was proposed. First, the data were fused as a combination of video and audio, then as a combination of audio and text as binary, and finally the results were fused together. The final output included audio, text and video data, taking into account common features. The convolutional neural network and long-term and short-term memory (CNN-LSTM) were then used to extract audio. Next, the Inception-Res Net-v2 network was used to extract facial expressions from the video. The output fused data were used by LSTM as the input of the Softmax classifier to recognise the emotion of audio and video features fusion. In addition, the CNN-LSTM was combined in the form of a binary channel for learning audio emotion features. Meanwhile, a Bi-LSTM network was used to extract the text features and Softmax was used to classify the fused features. Finally, the generated results were fused together for the final classification, and the logistic regression model was used for fusion and classification. As the results showed, the recognition accuracy of the proposed method on the IEMOCAP dataset was 82.9%.
**Keywords** Multimodal emotion · Fusion · LSTM · CNN · RNN · Machine learning · Audio processing · Text processing · Video processing

**3 The proposed method**
We propose a method that, like the structure of the human brain, selects the results derived from audio, text and image processing by selecting common and effective features for understanding the real emotion. In this context, we need a model capable of extracting effective features in a different way from existing algorithms. This paper presents a method for extracting effective features in audio and text, and a method for extracting effective features in audio and images. After extraction, the results of these two methods are merged through data fusion and used as input for the classifier.
**3.1 Proposed method architecture**
The proposed method architecture is shown in Fig. 1.
**3.1.1 Feature extraction method for audio and video**
The general architecture of the multimodal composite emotion recognition method for audio and video expressions using deep learning is shown in Fig. 2. In general, it is divided into feature extraction, feature selection and emotion classification modules.
The received input data must not be used for emotion categorisation without preparation. Therefore, the data mode should be changed. The separation module transforms the video data into audio and video data and then transforms the audio data into text. The feature extraction module forms the basis of the multimodal emotion recognition method, which aims to receive the input for information processing and transform it into the features that can be used in the model [22]. Different schemes are considered in the feature extraction module for extracting features. For audio, the long-term neural memory network (CNN-LSTM) is used, while for video, the Inception-Res Net-v2 network is used to extract the corresponding data. In a multifaceted emotional state, there is a correlation between LSTM structure and feature can be used for temporal dependence recognition from time series. In this respect, there is an informational relationship between different methods. These relationships can be used as common and hidden emotional cues between unimodal methods to help make decisions about the final emotion. LSTM captures the association of different methods and produces more accurate emotion recognition when there is little information or when the recognition results of two or more emotions are inconsistent. The extracted unimodal features are fed into the LSTM unit where the interdependence is captured. Following the feature selection process, the unimodal features are combined to form a composite feature. The LSTM structure is then used to extract the interdependence of the methods.
**Extraction of features from audio signals** Audio is a signal with a nonlinear time sequence feature, which is completely time-dependent. Meanwhile, the LSTM network is suitable for extracting audio features. When modelling information with context sensitivity, knowing the temporal information about the emotion feature of audio is very useful. However, there is no nonlinear hidden layer within the LSTM network, which increases the hidden mode coefficient. Overall, CNN and LSTM have limited capabilities and LSTM and CNN are applied for audio emotion recognition. Therefore, a combined network of LSTM and CNN is used here to learn audio emotional features. The structural features of the CNN

The correlation part consists of a maximum aggregation layer and two convolutional layers. The convolution layer has similar parameters to the CNN network parameters and a linear unit (ReLU) is used in the activation function [23]. The output of a set of CNNs feeds directly into LSTMs in the shared CNN-LSTM network. In this way, the advanced information including long-term contextual and local information dependencies can be obtained. However, CNNs leave a lot of data and focus on local information. A method using CNN and Bi-LSTM channels was presented to prevent the loss of valuable data. A set of four one-dimensional convolutional layers were used in the CNN channel with different numbers of filters for 1-D temporal input (audio features). In addition, the maximum pooling and general average pooling layers were applied to perform the average pooling and maximum pooling operations on the data. A set of Bi-LSTM cells with 256 arguments was placed in the Bi-LSTM channel to extract the information of long-term textual dependencies, and an attention mechanism was used to find more effective features. Finally, the data from the two channels were combined and the output was placed in a dense layer. After inducing the nonlinear change, the correlation of these features was determined and mapped to the output space [24] (Fig. 3).
**Face feature extraction** The amount of video data is usually very large. Therefore, we need to determine the face contour in each frame of the video and reduce the size of the frame image through face contour cropping, which is necessary for processing the data and obtaining the next features [25]. Here, the emotional information of the videos is determined by short-term feature extraction using InceptionRes Net-v2 network and signal Fourier transform (STFT) for deep feature extraction. The STFT is an audio signal processing tool that provides a very useful class of time–frequency distributions by specifying the signal amplitude that varies with frequency and time. The short-time Fourier transform is computed by dividing a long-time signal into shorter parts of

Inception-Res Net-v2 refers to a CNN developed by Google in 2016 by representing the ResNet network based on the Inception model, which has an accurate diagnostic effect on objects with high similarity. The network is considered a prototype of Inception V3, which uses the idea of connectivity in the Microsoft ResNet model, where the neural network receives deeper training. It is possible to significantly simplify the Inception module by using multiple 3 × 3 convolutions instead of 5 × 5 and 7 × 7 convolutions. As a result, the computational complexity and the dimensions of the parameters are significantly reduced and the training rate of the network is increased. The algorithm has a higher spatial complexity compared to other networks.

**3.2 Feature extraction scenario for audio and text** **features fusion (A/T)**
As shown in Fig. 4, the audio signal and text information are first processed to extract the features of low-level emotions. Then, the audio features are fed into the model to represent local and general information. To obtain high-level features, the textual features are added to Bi-LSTM neural networks. In the multimodal method, the DNN network is used for training and optimising the fusion features.
**3.2.1 Audio and text feature extraction**
**Audio feature extraction** The process starts by processing the raw audio signal using the data in the database. Then, 34-dimensional low-level audio features are extracted from spectral, temporal and cepstral domain features such as energy, zero crossing rate, energy entropy, spectral centre, spectral expansion, spectral entropy, spectral flux, spectral start and MFCC mel-frequency cepstral coefficients [29]. The maximum input of 100 frames is considered and the vector is obtained for each expression (100, 34). Many features such as MFCC, energy, zero-crossing rate and spectral flux are considered to represent the sensory characteristics of handheld acoustics.
**Text feature extraction** Word embedding is a popular method in text feature extraction by using dense vectors to represent the documents and words [30]. Word2vec is considered to be one of the most common word embedding methods. It is a way of generating a word matrix that combines the information of general and local statistics of words to obtain linguistic models and word vectors.

**4 Test and analysis**
After the preparation of the scenarios, the methods are used to test the accuracy of the feature extraction and the result of their fusion for a more accurate emotion recognition. The IEMOCAP database is used to perform the test and to analyse the results according to the steps described above.
**4.1 IEMOCAP emotion database**
The IEMOCAP emotion database [31] was used to evaluate the proposed method. The database contains almost 12 h of audiovisual data such as audio, video, facial movement recordings and text transcriptions.
**4.2 Chi-square test performance**

**4.4 Result and comparison**
**4.4.1 Result**
Some emotions are better recognised by speech, such as fear andsadness, whileothers arebetter recognisedbyvideo, such as happiness and anger. In voice emotion classification, anger and sadness are incorrectly recognised as happy and neutral expressions, while in facial expression classification, anger may be incorrectly recognised as sadness and happiness as neutral expression (Table 4). The text classifier recognises anger, happiness and neutrality very well. However, it is very difficult to distinguish between anger and sadness using text. One of the probable reasons for this difficulty is that both of these classes are negative and many similar words are used to express them. With the audio model, a higher level of accuracy was observed for the neutral and sad classes compared to text, but the difference was not as great as for the angry and happy
classes. Several happy cases were misclassified by the classifier. Nevertheless, the performance of the classifier was very good for discriminating between anger and sadness. In addition, some happy cases were misclassified as neutral. Although sad and angry faces could be classified effectively, the classifier showed some confused behaviour with sad and angry faces. The separation of neutral classes was more accurate compared to the other classes. However, there was some confusion with sad and happy faces. In the case of speech and text fusion, as well as speech and image, the recognition accuracy is higher than the unimodal model for all features, and the confusion is reduced in the case of misclassification. Trimodal and bimodal models perform better than unimodal models in several tests. In general, audio fusion performed well on all datasets.
**4.4.2 Comparison with other methods**
Mital et al. [30] proposed multimodal multiplicative emotion recognition (M3ER): first, feature vectors were extracted from three raw methods. Then, these features are fed to the model evaluation step to obtain the effective and ineffective features, and the former are used to build the proxy feature vectors. Finally, by fusing the selected features, they are used to determine the six emotions using the fusion of the final feature level with the attention module. The recognition accuracy of M3ER in IEMOCAP was 82.7%. The results showed that the recognition accuracy of the presented multimodal model outperformed the unimodal model and other multimodal models in the dataset.
**5 Conclusion**
A multimodal emotion recognition model was presented using audio, video and text from the IEMOCAP database. First, LSTM and two-channel CNN were used to determine the acoustic emotion features. Then, Bi-LSTM was used to extract the text features. Finally, a DNN was used to learn the fusion features. The model used deep learning networks, artificial and advanced features and took into account time and textual information in the data. L2 adaptation was also used to optimise the model. An (A/V) bimodal fusion was simultaneously used through deep learning using Long/Short-Term Memory Convolutional Neural Network andInception-ResNet-v2forextractingfacialexpressionfeatures in audio and video. In addition, the obtained features were fed into the LSTM unit and the individual methods were linked together to extract the fusion features using feature selection of chi-square test. The output feature data from the LSTM were then fed into the Softmax emotion recognition classifier. The results on the IEMOCAP dataset showed that
